questions.stem: When giving a bed bath to a resident, in which direction should the nurse aide wash the eye, and how should each eye be cleaned?

options.text: From the inner corner to the outer corner, using a clean area of the washcloth for each eye
From the inner corner outward, using soap and water on both eyes
From the outer corner to the inner corner, using the same part of the cloth for both eyes
In a circular scrubbing motion, reusing the same cloth area for each eye

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Wiping from the inner canthus to the outer corner moves debris away from the tear duct, and using a fresh part of the cloth for each eye prevents spreading infection from one eye to the other. Why the others are wrong: **C** wiping outer-to-inner pushes debris toward the duct and reusing the cloth cross-contaminates; **B** soap irritates the eyes and is not used on them; **D** scrubbing is rough and reusing the cloth area spreads microorganisms.

questions.stem: When providing oral care for a resident, what is the correct water temperature and the safest way to test it before use?

options.text: Very hot water to kill germs in the mouth
Comfortably warm water, with the temperature checked before bringing it to the resident
Any temperature, since the resident's mouth adjusts quickly
Cold water only, because warm water grows bacteria

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Oral care is done with comfortably warm water, and the aide should check the temperature first to protect the resident's delicate oral tissues from burns. Why the others are wrong: **A** very hot water can scald the mouth; **D** germs are removed by cleaning, not by using cold water, which is unnecessarily uncomfortable; **C** ignoring temperature risks injuring fragile mucous membranes.

questions.stem: A resident has weakness on the left side after a stroke. When helping the resident put on a shirt, which arm should the nurse aide dress first?

options.text: Whichever arm the resident points to
Both arms at the same time to save time
The left (weaker) arm first
The right (stronger) arm first

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The weaker (affected) side is dressed first and undressed last, which puts less stress and stretch on the impaired limb and makes dressing easier. Why the others are wrong: **D** dressing the strong arm first forces the weak arm through a fully fitted sleeve, which is harder and can cause injury; **A** the rule is based on limb function, not preference; **B** dressing both arms at once is not possible and ignores the affected-side principle.

questions.stem: A resident with dentures finishes a meal. What is the safest way for the nurse aide to clean the dentures?

options.text: Wrap them in a dry tissue and store them in the resident's pocket
Brush them while holding them over an empty, hard sink
Scrub them with hot water to disinfect them quickly
Hold them over a sink lined with a towel or filled with water while brushing them

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Lining the sink with a towel or water cushions the dentures so they will not break if they slip from the aide's hands. Why the others are wrong: **C** hot water can warp dentures; **B** an empty hard sink offers no cushion, so a dropped denture shatters; **A** a dry tissue can be mistaken for trash and the dentures may dry out or be lost.

questions.stem: A resident on a thickened-liquid diet is at risk for choking. Which feeding practice best promotes safe swallowing?

options.text: Position the resident sitting upright and offer small amounts, allowing time to swallow between bites
Have the resident lie back flat so gravity helps the food go down
Encourage the resident to eat quickly before the food cools
Give large spoonfuls so the meal is finished sooner

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Sitting upright with small bites and adequate time between them reduces the risk of aspiration and choking. Why the others are wrong: **B** lying flat makes aspiration far more likely; **C** rushing increases choking risk; **D** large spoonfuls overwhelm the resident's ability to swallow safely.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is recording a resident's fluid intake. The resident drank an 8-ounce (240 mL) cup of juice. How should this be documented?

options.text: Do not record it because juice is not counted as fluid intake
Record 240 mL on the intake and output (I&O) record
Record it only if the resident asks for more fluids
Estimate it as 'about a cup' in the nurse's verbal report

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Fluids consumed are measured and recorded accurately in milliliters on the I&O record so the care team can monitor hydration. Why the others are wrong: **C** intake is recorded regardless of whether the resident requests more; **D** documentation must be precise, not a vague estimate; **A** juice and other liquids absolutely count as fluid intake.

questions.stem: A resident uses a bedpan but is embarrassed and wants privacy. After positioning the resident safely on the bedpan, what should the nurse aide do?

options.text: Tell the resident that privacy is not allowed during toileting
Leave the room and return in 30 minutes regardless of the resident's needs
Provide privacy and a way to call for help, then step out or behind the curtain unless the resident is unsafe to leave
Stand at the bedside watching the resident the entire time

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Toileting should preserve dignity by giving privacy and the call light, while keeping the resident safe and within reach of help. Why the others are wrong: **D** standing and watching humiliates the resident; **B** a fixed 30-minute absence ignores the resident's actual needs and safety; **A** residents always have a right to privacy during personal care.

questions.stem: A resident has an indwelling urinary catheter. To help prevent infection and maintain proper drainage, where should the nurse aide keep the drainage bag?

options.text: Attached to the side rail at chest height
On the resident's lap during transfers
Above the level of the bladder so urine drains faster
Below the level of the bladder and not resting on the floor

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The drainage bag is kept below bladder level so urine flows downward by gravity and does not backflow, and off the floor to avoid contamination. Why the others are wrong: **C** a bag above the bladder lets urine flow back toward the bladder, raising infection risk; **B** placing the bag on the lap raises it above the bladder; **A** chest height is above the bladder and promotes backflow.

questions.stem: A nurse aide wants to promote restful sleep for a resident at night. Which two actions best support this goal? (Select two.)

options.text: Reduce noise and dim the lights in the resident's room
Turn on bright overhead lights to check on the resident frequently
Offer a back rub or help the resident get into a comfortable position
Serve a large caffeinated drink right before bedtime

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** A quiet, dimly lit room and comfort measures such as a back rub or repositioning promote relaxation and restful sleep. Why the others are wrong: **D** caffeine is a stimulant that interferes with sleep; **B** bright lights and frequent disruptive checks disturb sleep rather than support it.

questions.stem: What is the single most effective action a nurse aide can take to prevent the spread of infection between residents?

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before and after caring for each resident
Wear the same pair of gloves for several residents in a row
Open windows to let fresh air circulate
Spray air freshener in each resident's room

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Hand hygiene before and after each resident contact is the single most important measure for preventing the transmission of infection. Why the others are wrong: **B** reusing gloves between residents spreads germs and never replaces hand hygiene; **C** ventilation does not stop contact transmission of pathogens; **D** air freshener masks odor but does nothing to control infection.

questions.stem: Under standard precautions, in which two situations should a nurse aide wear gloves? (Select two.)

options.text: When emptying a urinary drainage bag or handling a bedpan
When providing perineal (peri) care that may involve contact with body fluids
When combing a resident's hair and assisting with dressing
When feeding a resident who needs help with a meal

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Standard precautions require gloves whenever contact with blood or body fluids is likely, which includes perineal care and emptying a drainage bag or handling a bedpan. Why the others are wrong: **D** feeding a resident does not involve expected contact with body fluids, so gloves are not routinely required; **C** combing hair and helping with dressing are dry tasks with no anticipated body-fluid contact.

questions.stem: When removing soiled disposable gloves after care, what technique should the nurse aide use to avoid contaminating the hands?

options.text: Wash the gloves with soap and keep wearing them for the next task
Peel each glove off so it turns inside out, with the dirty surface contained inside
Pull the gloves off by the fingertips so the outside stays facing out
Blow into the gloves to loosen them, then set them aside to reuse

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Gloves are removed so they turn inside out, trapping the contaminated surface inside and away from the skin. Why the others are wrong: **C** pulling from the fingertips leaves the soiled outer surface exposed and likely to touch the skin; **D** disposable gloves are single-use and are discarded, not reused; **A** washing and reusing disposable gloves does not make them safe and spreads contamination.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is putting on personal protective equipment (PPE) before entering an isolation room. Place the steps in the correct donning order.

options.text: Put on the gown and tie it at the neck and waist
Put on the mask or respirator and secure it
Put on goggles or a face shield
Put on gloves, pulling them over the gown cuffs

questions.explanation: The correct donning sequence is gown first, then mask or respirator, then goggles or face shield, and gloves last. The gown is applied first because it covers the most skin and clothing. The mask and eye protection go on next to protect the face. Gloves are donned last and pulled over the gown's cuffs so the wrists are sealed and no skin is exposed; putting gloves on earlier would let them be contaminated while adjusting other equipment.

questions.stem: A nurse aide finds a resident has slid down and is sitting on the floor next to the bed, awake and talking. What should the aide do first?

options.text: Leave to find a wheelchair before doing anything else
Immediately lift the resident back into bed alone
Stay with the resident, check for injury, and call the nurse before moving the resident
Help the resident stand quickly so no one sees the fall

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** After a fall the aide stays with the resident, checks for injury, and notifies the nurse, who assesses the resident before any move. Why the others are wrong: **B** lifting alone can worsen an unseen injury and injure the aide; **A** leaving the resident alone on the floor is unsafe; **D** rushing the resident up to hide the fall risks harm and violates honest reporting.

questions.stem: Using good body mechanics, how should a nurse aide lift a heavy object from the floor?

options.text: Twist at the waist while lifting to move the object to the side
Keep the legs straight and bend at the waist to reach the object
Hold the object at arm's length away from the body
Bend at the knees and hips and lift with the leg muscles, keeping the back straight

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Proper body mechanics use the strong leg muscles by bending the knees and hips while keeping the back straight, which protects the spine. Why the others are wrong: **B** bending at the waist with straight legs strains the lower back; **A** twisting while lifting is a common cause of back injury; **C** holding a load away from the body increases strain rather than keeping it close.

questions.stem: A resident begins to cough forcefully and is able to speak while eating. What is the most appropriate first action by the nurse aide?

options.text: Encourage the resident to keep coughing, since coughing can clear the airway
Begin abdominal thrusts immediately
Give the resident a large drink of water to wash the food down
Lay the resident flat on the back

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A person who can cough forcefully and speak has a partial airway obstruction with adequate air movement; encouraging continued coughing is the correct response. Why the others are wrong: **B** abdominal thrusts are for a complete obstruction when the person cannot cough, speak, or breathe; **C** fluids can worsen choking and cause aspiration; **D** lying flat does not relieve the obstruction and may make it worse.

questions.stem: A fire breaks out in a resident care area. Arrange the steps of the RACE fire-response sequence in the correct order.

options.text: Rescue residents in immediate danger and move them to safety
Alarm: activate the fire alarm and alert others
Confine the fire by closing doors and windows
Extinguish a small fire if safe, or evacuate as directed

questions.explanation: RACE orders the response Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish. Rescuing anyone in immediate danger comes first because protecting life is the top priority. Activating the alarm next brings help and warns others. Confining the fire by closing doors and windows slows its spread and starves it of oxygen. Extinguishing a small fire (or evacuating) is last, attempted only when people are safe and the alarm has been sounded.

questions.stem: Where should a nurse aide place an electronic blood pressure cuff or position the stethoscope to take a manual blood pressure on the upper arm?

options.text: Over the radial artery at the wrist
Over the brachial artery, with the cuff snug about one inch above the bend of the elbow
Directly over the bend of the elbow with the cuff loose
On the forearm midway between the wrist and elbow

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An upper-arm blood pressure is measured over the brachial artery with the cuff placed snugly about an inch above the antecubital (elbow) crease. Why the others are wrong: **A** the radial artery at the wrist is used for the pulse, not an upper-arm cuff; **C** a loose cuff placed right over the elbow gives an inaccurate reading; **D** the mid-forearm is not the correct site for the brachial artery.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is taking an apical pulse on a resident. Where is the stethoscope placed and for how long is the pulse counted?

options.text: At the wrist over the radial artery for one full minute
Over the carotid artery in the neck for 15 seconds
Over the apex of the heart on the left side of the chest, counted for one full minute
On the right side of the chest for 30 seconds

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The apical pulse is heard with a stethoscope over the apex of the heart (left side of the chest) and counted for one full minute for accuracy. Why the others are wrong: **B** the carotid is palpated, not used for the apical pulse, and a full minute is the standard for apical counts; **D** the heart's apex is on the left, not the right; **A** the radial site is a peripheral pulse, not the apical pulse.

questions.stem: When measuring a resident's weight on a standing scale, which practice gives the most accurate and consistent reading over time?

options.text: Weigh the resident at random times with whatever they are wearing
Add a few pounds to account for clothing without checking
Skip balancing the scale to save time
Weigh the resident at about the same time of day wearing similar clothing, with the scale balanced at zero

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Consistent weights require the same time of day, similar clothing, and a scale zeroed (balanced) before use so trends are meaningful. Why the others are wrong: **A** random conditions produce unreliable comparisons; **B** guessing a clothing allowance introduces error; **C** failing to zero the scale gives an inaccurate reading.

questions.stem: A nurse aide takes a resident's oral temperature and reads 101.4°F (38.6°C). What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Record the temperature and report the elevated reading to the nurse
Decide the resident has an infection and start extra fluids on the aide's own judgment
Ignore it because temperatures naturally vary
Re-take it repeatedly until it reads normal

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The aide accurately records the measurement and reports an abnormal value like an elevated temperature to the nurse, who evaluates it. Why the others are wrong: **B** diagnosing an infection and changing care are outside the aide's scope; **C** an elevated temperature is a meaningful change that must be reported, not ignored; **D** repeating the measurement to force a normal result falsifies the data.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of objective data a nurse aide would report to the nurse?

options.text: The resident says, 'I feel dizzy'
The resident's pulse is 96 beats per minute
The resident reports feeling nauseated
The resident states the pain is a 7 out of 10

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Objective data are observable and measurable, such as a counted pulse rate of 96. Why the others are wrong: **A**, **C**, and **D** are all subjective data—statements of what the resident feels (dizziness, nausea, and a self-rated pain level) that cannot be directly observed by the aide.

questions.stem: A nurse aide repositions a bed-bound resident regularly. What is the main reason for changing a resident's position at least every two hours?

options.text: To keep the bed linens from wrinkling
To make the room look tidy for visitors
To relieve pressure on the skin and help prevent pressure injuries (bedsores)
To give the aide regular exercise

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Regular repositioning relieves prolonged pressure over bony areas, restoring circulation and helping prevent pressure injuries. Why the others are wrong: **A** smooth linens help comfort but are not the main reason for repositioning; **D** the purpose is resident skin health, not aide exercise; **B** appearance for visitors is irrelevant to the clinical purpose.

questions.stem: Which two findings should a nurse aide report to the nurse promptly because they may signal a developing problem? (Select two.)

options.text: The resident ate all of breakfast and is in a good mood
A sudden change in the resident's mental status, such as new confusion
A new reddened area over the resident's tailbone that does not fade
The resident watched television in the afternoon

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, C):** A new non-blanching reddened area can be an early pressure injury, and a sudden change in mental status can signal infection or another acute problem; both must be reported. Why the others are wrong: **A** a good appetite and mood are normal findings, not warning signs; **D** watching television is an ordinary activity that needs no report.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is assigned to apply a warm compress but realizes the procedure was not covered in training and is unfamiliar. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Attempt the procedure anyway to avoid looking incapable
Skip the task and say nothing to anyone
Ask another resident's family member how to do it
Tell the nurse the aide has not been trained on the task and ask for guidance

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A nurse aide must only perform tasks for which they are trained and competent; when unsure, the aide informs the nurse and asks for direction. Why the others are wrong: **A** performing an unfamiliar procedure can harm the resident; **C** a family member is not a proper or reliable source of clinical instruction; **B** silently skipping a delegated task neglects the resident's care.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of performing range-of-motion (ROM) exercises with a resident who has limited mobility?

options.text: To maintain joint flexibility and prevent stiffness and contractures
To replace the resident's prescribed medications
To keep the resident in bed for longer periods
To build large muscles and increase the resident's weight

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** ROM exercises move joints through their normal motion to maintain flexibility and prevent stiffness and contractures. Why the others are wrong: **D** ROM maintains mobility, not bodybuilding or weight gain; **B** exercises do not replace medications; **C** ROM promotes movement and function, not extended bed rest.

questions.stem: While performing passive range-of-motion exercises, the nurse aide moves a resident's joint and the resident reports pain. What should the aide do?

options.text: Move the joint quickly so the pain is over sooner
Stop at the point of pain, avoid forcing the joint, and report the pain to the nurse
Continue the full exercise and ignore the complaint
Push the joint past the pain to improve flexibility faster

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Joints are moved slowly and only to the point of resistance or mild discomfort; the aide stops at pain, never forces the joint, and reports it. Why the others are wrong: **D** forcing past pain can injure the joint; **C** ignoring pain risks harm and misses a finding that should be reported; **A** moving quickly can cause injury and does not relieve the underlying pain.

questions.stem: A resident is learning to walk again using a walker. Which approach by the nurse aide best supports the resident's independence and rehabilitation?

options.text: Do the walking task for the resident to save time
Keep the resident in a wheelchair so they do not have to try
Encourage and allow the resident to do as much as safely possible, giving help only as needed
Tell the resident that using the walker is pointless

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Restorative care promotes independence by letting residents do as much as they safely can while the aide assists only as needed. Why the others are wrong: **A** doing the task for the resident fosters dependence and works against rehabilitation; **D** discouraging the resident undermines motivation and recovery; **B** unnecessary wheelchair use removes the chance to regain function.

questions.stem: A resident with dementia becomes increasingly agitated and restless in the late afternoon. What is an appropriate first response by the nurse aide?

options.text: Physically restrain the resident to stop the restlessness
Leave the resident alone in a busy, noisy hallway
Argue with the resident to correct their confused statements
Stay calm, speak gently, and try to reduce noise and other triggers in the environment

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A calm, reassuring approach with reduced environmental triggers helps de-escalate agitation in residents with dementia (sometimes called sundowning). Why the others are wrong: **C** arguing increases distress and confusion; **B** a busy, noisy setting worsens agitation; **A** restraints require an order and are never a first response, and can cause harm.

questions.stem: A resident recently lost a spouse and is tearful and withdrawn. Which response by the nurse aide is most supportive?

options.text: Sit with the resident, listen, and allow them to express their feelings
Tell the resident their feelings are not important
Change the subject every time the spouse is mentioned
Tell the resident to stop crying and cheer up

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Grief is supported by being present, listening, and allowing the resident to express emotions without judgment. Why the others are wrong: **D** dismissing the tears denies the resident's grief; **C** avoiding the topic blocks healthy expression of loss; **B** belittling the resident's feelings is disrespectful and harmful.

questions.stem: Which behavior change should the nurse aide report as a possible sign of depression in a resident?

options.text: Choosing to attend a favorite weekly social group
Loss of interest in activities, withdrawal, and a change in appetite or sleep
Asking for help putting on a sweater because the room is cold
Smiling and chatting with a roommate

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Withdrawal, loss of interest in usual activities, and changes in appetite or sleep are recognized warning signs of depression that should be reported. Why the others are wrong: **A** attending a favorite group is healthy engagement; **D** socializing and smiling are positive signs; **C** requesting a sweater for comfort is a normal, reasonable request.

questions.stem: Which two actions by the nurse aide best promote a resident's dignity and self-esteem during personal care? (Select two.)

options.text: Talk about the resident with coworkers as if the resident were not present
Offer choices when possible, such as what to wear or when to bathe
Address the resident by their preferred name and explain care before doing it
Rush through care without telling the resident what is happening

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, C):** Using the resident's preferred name and explaining care shows respect, and offering choices preserves autonomy; both support dignity and self-esteem. Why the others are wrong: **A** talking over the resident as if absent is demeaning; **D** rushing without explanation is disrespectful and frightening.

questions.stem: A resident's religious practice forbids eating pork, and pork is on the day's menu. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse aide?

options.text: Tell the resident that the kitchen does not make exceptions
Remove the meal and offer nothing in its place
Respect the resident's belief and inform the nurse or dietary staff so an alternative is provided
Encourage the resident to eat the pork this one time

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The aide respects the resident's religious dietary restriction and arranges an acceptable alternative through the nurse or dietary department. Why the others are wrong: **D** pressuring the resident to violate a belief is disrespectful; **A** dismissing the request ignores the resident's rights and needs; **B** leaving the resident without food fails to meet their nutritional needs.

questions.stem: A resident wishes to see a clergy member and spend time in prayer. How should the nurse aide respond?

options.text: Tell the resident that prayer is not allowed in the facility
Decide the resident does not really need spiritual support
Interrupt the prayer frequently to complete routine tasks
Support the request, provide privacy, and inform the nurse so a visit can be arranged

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Residents have the right to practice their faith; the aide supports the request, ensures privacy, and notifies the nurse to help arrange a clergy visit. Why the others are wrong: **A** residents are entitled to religious expression; **B** it is not the aide's place to judge a resident's spiritual needs; **C** repeatedly interrupting prayer is disrespectful of the resident's beliefs.

questions.stem: A resident is hard of hearing and does not use a hearing aid. Which two communication techniques are most helpful? (Select two.)

options.text: Cover your mouth while talking so the resident is not distracted
Shout loudly from across the room
Reduce background noise, such as turning down the television
Face the resident and speak clearly at a normal-to-slightly-slower pace

questions.explanation: **Correct (C, D):** Facing the resident and speaking clearly lets them hear and read lips, and reducing background noise removes competing sound. Why the others are wrong: **B** shouting distorts speech and can seem aggressive; **A** covering the mouth prevents lip reading and muffles the sound.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of nonverbal communication a nurse aide should be aware of when interacting with residents?

options.text: Facial expressions, body posture, and tone of voice
The room number on the door
The exact words written in the care plan
The medication list on the chart

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Nonverbal communication includes facial expressions, body posture, gestures, and tone of voice, which all convey meaning beyond words. Why the others are wrong: **C** care-plan wording is written verbal communication; **D** a medication list is documented information, not nonverbal cues; **B** a room number is a label, not communication between people.

questions.stem: Which technique demonstrates therapeutic, active listening when a resident is speaking about a concern?

options.text: Look at the clock and check the time repeatedly
Make eye contact, allow the resident to finish, and reflect back what was heard
Finish the resident's sentences to move things along
Change the topic to something more pleasant

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Active, therapeutic listening means giving full attention, making eye contact, letting the resident finish, and reflecting back to confirm understanding. Why the others are wrong: **C** finishing sentences interrupts and assumes meaning; **A** clock-watching signals disinterest; **D** changing the subject dismisses the resident's concern.

questions.stem: A resident refuses to take a bath this morning. What is the nurse aide's most appropriate response?

options.text: Bathe the resident anyway because it is on the schedule
Tell the resident they will lose privileges if they refuse
Respect the resident's right to refuse, try to learn why, and report the refusal to the nurse
Document that the bath was completed even though it was not

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Residents have the right to refuse care; the aide respects the refusal, explores the reason, may offer it later, and reports to the nurse. Why the others are wrong: **A** forcing a bath violates the resident's rights and can be battery; **B** threatening loss of privileges is coercion; **D** charting care that was not given is falsification.

questions.stem: Which two actions help a nurse aide protect a resident's right to privacy during personal care? (Select two.)

options.text: Leave the door open so coworkers can watch and learn
Keep the resident covered, exposing only the body area being cared for
Close the door and pull the privacy curtain before beginning care
Discuss the resident's care loudly in the hallway afterward

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, C):** Closing the door and curtain and keeping the resident covered—exposing only the area being cared for—protects bodily privacy and dignity. Why the others are wrong: **A** leaving the door open exposes the resident to onlookers; **D** discussing care loudly in public breaches confidentiality.

questions.stem: A resident is restless and keeps trying to get out of bed. The nurse aide believes a vest restraint would keep the resident safe. What should the aide do?

options.text: Apply a vest restraint on the aide's own judgment to prevent a fall
Tie the resident's wrists loosely to the bed rails
Lock the resident's door so they cannot leave the room
Not apply any restraint; instead try alternatives, supervise the resident, and report the behavior to the nurse

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Residents have the right to be free from unnecessary restraint; restraints require a physician's order and are a last resort, so the aide uses alternatives and reports to the nurse. Why the others are wrong: **A** an aide cannot apply a restraint on personal judgment without an order; **B** tying the wrists is an unauthorized restraint that can cause serious injury; **C** locking a resident in a room is illegal confinement.

questions.stem: A resident keeps a few personal photographs and a small clock on the bedside table. How should the nurse aide treat these items?

options.text: Treat them as the resident's personal possessions, handle them with care, and do not move or discard them without permission
Throw them away to reduce clutter
Move them to another resident's room
Take them home because they look unimportant

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Residents have the right to keep and have their personal possessions respected; the aide handles them carefully and does not move or remove them without permission. Why the others are wrong: **B** discarding a resident's belongings violates their rights; **C** moving items to another room is improper handling of personal property; **D** taking a resident's possessions is theft.

questions.stem: A nurse aide notices unexplained bruising on a resident and overhears a coworker speaking harshly and threatening the resident. What is the aide's legal and ethical duty?

options.text: Confront and discipline the coworker personally
Report the suspected abuse to the nurse or supervisor immediately
Keep quiet to avoid causing trouble for a coworker
Wait several days to see if it happens again before saying anything

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Nurse aides are mandatory reporters and must report suspected abuse or neglect to the nurse or supervisor immediately. Why the others are wrong: **C** staying silent makes the aide complicit and violates the duty to report; **A** disciplining a coworker is not the aide's role and can endanger the resident; **D** delaying a report leaves the resident at continued risk.

questions.stem: A resident's neighbor approaches a nurse aide in the community and asks about the resident's medical condition. How should the aide respond to protect confidentiality (HIPAA)?

options.text: Share the diagnosis because the neighbor seems concerned
Tell the neighbor to ask other residents for the information
Politely decline to share any information, since resident health information is confidential
Give general details as long as the resident's name is not used in writing

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Resident health information is confidential under HIPAA and is shared only with the care team on a need-to-know basis, so the aide does not disclose it to a neighbor. Why the others are wrong: **A** good intentions do not authorize disclosure; **D** sharing details verbally still breaches confidentiality even without a written name; **B** directing the neighbor to other residents spreads private information further.

questions.stem: A nurse aide notices an instruction on the care plan that seems unclear. What is the best action?

options.text: Ignore the care plan and do what seems easiest
Guess at what the care plan means and proceed
Change the care plan to match the aide's own preference
Ask the nurse for clarification before carrying out the task

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The aide works under the nurse's supervision and follows the care plan; when something is unclear, the aide asks the nurse for clarification before acting. Why the others are wrong: **B** guessing can lead to errors and harm; **A** ignoring the care plan abandons the resident's individualized care; **C** the aide is not authorized to change the care plan.

questions.stem: A nurse aide has many residents to care for during a busy shift. Which two actions reflect good time management and professionalism? (Select two.)

options.text: Complete only the tasks the aide enjoys and leave the rest undone
Rush care and skip steps to finish everything quickly
Communicate with the team and ask for help when the workload is unsafe
Prioritize tasks based on residents' needs and the care plan

questions.explanation: **Correct (C, D):** Good time management means prioritizing by resident need and the care plan, and communicating with the team to ask for help when the workload becomes unsafe. Why the others are wrong: **B** rushing and skipping steps compromises safety and quality; **A** doing only preferred tasks neglects residents who still need care.

questions.stem: When giving a complete bed bath, in what general order should the nurse aide wash the body to keep the water cleanest the longest?

options.text: From the cleanest areas, such as the face, to the dirtiest areas, such as the perineum, last
From the dirtiest areas to the cleanest areas
In any order, since the water is changed after every body part
Feet first and face last to save the freshest water for the legs

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A bed bath proceeds from the cleanest areas (face and eyes) toward the dirtiest (the perineum and rectal area last) so cleaner water is used on cleaner skin and contamination is not spread upward. Why the others are wrong: **B** washing dirtiest-first spreads microorganisms onto cleaner skin; **D** saving fresh water for the legs ignores the face, the cleanest area, which is washed first; **C** the basin water is not realistically changed after every single part, so order still matters.

questions.stem: A resident has long, thick toenails. The nurse aide notices the resident also has diabetes. What is the correct action regarding the toenails?

options.text: Trim and file the toenails as part of routine foot care
Cut the nails very short to prevent ingrown nails
Do not cut the toenails; report the need to the nurse, as nail care for a diabetic resident is not done by the aide
Soak the feet in hot water and then clip the nails

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A nurse aide does not cut the toenails of a resident with diabetes (or poor circulation) because a small nick can lead to a serious, slow-healing infection; the aide reports the need to the nurse. Why the others are wrong: **A** routine clipping is unsafe for a diabetic resident; **B** cutting nails very short raises the risk of injury and ingrown nails; **D** hot water can burn a diabetic resident who may have reduced sensation, and the aide still should not clip the nails.

questions.stem: A resident needs help eating and is visually impaired. To help the resident locate food on the plate, what technique should the nurse aide use?

options.text: Mix all the foods together so they are easier to scoop
Feed the resident quickly without saying what each bite is
Tell the resident to find the food on their own
Describe the food using clock positions, such as 'meat at 6 o'clock, vegetables at 9 o'clock'

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Describing the plate as the face of a clock helps a visually impaired resident locate each food and eat with dignity and independence. Why the others are wrong: **A** mixing foods together removes choice and is unappetizing; **B** feeding without describing the food denies the resident control and information; **C** giving no orientation leaves a visually impaired resident unable to find the food safely.

questions.stem: A resident is constipated and the care plan encourages a normal bowel pattern. Which measure is within the nurse aide's role to help promote regular elimination?

options.text: Give the resident an over-the-counter laxative
Encourage fluids, fiber from the ordered diet, and activity, and offer toileting on a regular schedule
Administer an enema without an order
Tell the resident to simply hold it until the urge passes

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Encouraging fluids, dietary fiber, activity, and regular toileting are aide-appropriate measures that support normal bowel function. Why the others are wrong: **A** giving a laxative is administering medication, which is outside the aide's scope; **C** an enema requires an order and is not an aide-initiated action; **D** ignoring the urge to defecate worsens constipation.

questions.stem: A resident has an ostomy with a colostomy bag. When emptying the bag, what should the nurse aide do, and what must be reported to the nurse?

options.text: Empty the bag wearing gloves and report any redness, breakdown, or bleeding of the skin around the stoma
Empty the bag without gloves, since stool in a bag is not a body fluid
Change the entire ostomy appliance and clip away loose skin
Leave a full bag in place until the next shift

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The aide empties the ostomy bag using gloves under standard precautions and reports any redness, skin breakdown, or bleeding around the stoma to the nurse. Why the others are wrong: **B** stool is a body fluid and gloves are required; **C** assessing the stoma and altering skin is outside the aide's scope; **D** leaving a full bag risks leakage, odor, and skin irritation.

questions.stem: A male resident needs help shaving with a safety razor. Which practice is correct for safe shaving?

options.text: Soften the beard with warm water or lather and shave in the direction the hair grows, holding the skin taut
Shave against the direction of hair growth using a dry face
Press the razor hard to finish faster
Reuse another resident's razor if a clean one is not handy

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Softening the beard and shaving in the direction of hair growth while holding the skin taut prevents nicks and irritation. Why the others are wrong: **B** shaving a dry face against the grain causes cuts and razor burn; **C** pressing hard increases the risk of cutting the skin; **D** sharing razors can transmit bloodborne pathogens and is never done.

questions.stem: A resident has a urinary catheter and the aide is providing perineal care. Which two practices help keep the resident clean and prevent infection? (Select two.)

options.text: Clean the perineal area from front to back (clean to dirty)
Clean from the rectal area toward the urethra
Clean a few inches of the catheter tubing moving away from the body, the way the care plan directs
Pull on the catheter to test that it is secure

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Cleaning front to back keeps stool away from the urethra, and cleaning the catheter from the body outward (away from the insertion site) removes secretions without pushing germs toward the bladder. Why the others are wrong: **B** wiping back-to-front drags rectal bacteria toward the urethra and raises infection risk; **D** tugging on the catheter can injure the resident and dislodge it.

questions.stem: A resident is on a fluid-restriction order. The resident repeatedly asks for more water. What should the nurse aide do?

options.text: Give the resident as much water as requested
Tell the resident to stop asking for water
Remove all fluids from the room so the resident cannot drink
Provide frequent mouth care and offer ice chips within the ordered limit, and report the resident's thirst to the nurse

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Within a fluid restriction, the aide eases thirst with mouth care and small amounts of ice chips (counted toward intake) and reports the resident's discomfort to the nurse. Why the others are wrong: **A** exceeding the restriction can harm a resident with heart or kidney problems; **B** dismissing the resident is unkind and ignores a real need; **C** removing all fluids is excessive and demeaning, and does not address the thirst.

questions.stem: A resident complains of being too warm at night and cannot sleep. Which comfort measure is the most appropriate first step for the nurse aide?

options.text: Adjust the bedding and room temperature and offer lighter covers for comfort
Give the resident a sleeping pill
Tell the resident that being warm is normal and to ignore it
Open an outside window wide in cold weather and leave the resident uncovered

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Promoting comfort and sleep starts with simple measures the aide controls, such as adjusting bedding, room temperature, and offering lighter covers. Why the others are wrong: **B** giving any medication is outside the aide's scope; **C** dismissing the complaint ignores a comfort need that affects sleep; **D** leaving the resident uncovered with a wide-open window in cold weather risks chilling and is unsafe.

questions.stem: A resident is on contact precautions for a multidrug-resistant organism. Where should the nurse aide remove the gown and gloves, and what is done next?

options.text: Remove gown and gloves inside the room before leaving, then perform hand hygiene
Wear the gown and gloves to the next resident's room to save supplies
Remove them in the hallway after leaving the room
Keep the same gown on all shift and change only the gloves

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Contaminated PPE is removed inside the resident's room (or at the doorway) before leaving, followed by hand hygiene, so pathogens stay contained. Why the others are wrong: **B** wearing PPE to another room transfers the organism; **C** removing PPE in the hallway has already spread contamination outside the room; **D** reusing a gown across the shift defeats the purpose of contact precautions.

questions.stem: A resident uses a transfer (gait) belt to stand and walk. Where is the belt applied, and how should it fit?

options.text: Around the neck, fitted loosely
Around the chest, as tight as possible
Around the hips on bare skin
Around the waist over clothing, snug enough to grasp but not so tight it restricts breathing

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A gait belt is applied around the waist over clothing and fitted snugly—tight enough to grasp securely yet still allowing the resident to breathe. Why the others are wrong: **A** a neck belt could choke the resident; **B** a chest belt fitted as tight as possible restricts breathing; **C** placing the belt on bare skin can pinch and is uncomfortable and unsafe.

questions.stem: A resident with weakness on one side is transferring from the bed to a wheelchair. On which side should the wheelchair be placed?

options.text: On the resident's weaker (affected) side
Directly behind the resident
On the resident's stronger side so they move toward their strong side
It does not matter which side the wheelchair is on

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The wheelchair is positioned on the resident's stronger side so they pivot and bear weight toward the strong side, making the transfer safer. Why the others are wrong: **A** moving toward the weak side gives the resident no stable side to lead with; **B** placing the chair behind the resident blocks a controlled pivot; **D** side placement matters greatly for a safe, balanced transfer.

questions.stem: A nurse aide takes a resting respiratory rate. To get an accurate count, what should the aide do?

options.text: Tell the resident you are counting their breaths and ask them to breathe normally
Count only for 5 seconds and multiply by 12
Count respirations without telling the resident, ideally right after taking the pulse while still holding the wrist
Ask the resident how many times per minute they think they breathe

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Respirations are counted without the resident's awareness—often right after the pulse while still holding the wrist—because people change their breathing when they know it is being watched. Why the others are wrong: **A** telling the resident makes them alter their breathing; **B** a 5-second count is too short to be accurate for respirations; **D** the resident's guess is not a measured count.

questions.stem: Which set of vital sign findings is generally within normal limits for a resting adult and would NOT require an urgent report to the nurse?

options.text: Oral temperature 98.6°F (37°C), pulse 78, respirations 16
Pulse 142 and irregular at rest
Respirations 6 per minute
Oral temperature 103.8°F (39.9°C)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A temperature of 98.6°F, pulse of 78, and 16 respirations all fall within typical adult resting ranges (about 97–99°F, pulse 60–100, respirations 12–20). Why the others are wrong: **B** a pulse of 142 is far above the normal resting range and is reported; **C** 6 respirations is dangerously low and must be reported; **D** 103.8°F is a high fever requiring prompt reporting.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is measuring a bedfast resident's height. What is the correct method?

options.text: Estimate the height by looking at the resident
Use a tape measure with the resident lying straight, marking from the top of the head to the bottom of the heels
Have the resident stand on the bed and use a wall chart
Record the height from last year without measuring

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** For a resident who cannot stand, height is measured with a tape measure while the resident lies straight in bed, marking the linens at the top of the head and the bottom of the heels. Why the others are wrong: **A** estimating by sight is inaccurate; **C** having a bedfast resident stand on the bed is unsafe; **D** copying an old value is falsifying the measurement.

questions.stem: A resident suddenly slumps, has slurred speech, and a drooping face. What should the nurse aide do first?

options.text: Give the resident food and water to boost their energy
Stay with the resident, call for the nurse and emergency help immediately, and note the time symptoms began
Walk the resident around to improve circulation
Wait an hour to see whether the symptoms resolve on their own

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Slurred speech and facial drooping are warning signs of a possible stroke; the aide stays with the resident, summons the nurse and emergency help at once, and notes the time of onset because rapid treatment is critical. Why the others are wrong: **A** giving food or fluids risks aspiration and delays care; **C** walking the resident is unsafe and wastes critical time; **D** waiting can cause permanent harm in a time-sensitive emergency.

questions.stem: Which two practices help prevent falls for residents in a long-term care setting? (Select two.)

options.text: Keep the call light, water, and personal items within the resident's reach
Leave spills on the floor for housekeeping to find later
Make sure the resident wears nonskid footwear and the bed is at a safe low position with brakes locked
Keep the room dimly lit at all hours to encourage rest

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Keeping needed items within reach reduces risky reaching and getting up, and nonskid footwear plus a low, locked bed give a stable, safe base. Why the others are wrong: **B** leaving spills creates a slip hazard; **D** poor lighting at all hours makes it hard to see obstacles and increases fall risk.

questions.stem: A nurse aide notices that a resident's reading glasses are smudged and the call light cord is frayed. What is the best action regarding the frayed cord?

options.text: Continue using it since it still works
Tape over the frayed area and keep using it
Take the device out of service and report it to the nurse or maintenance so it can be repaired or replaced
Cut off the call light so the resident cannot use it

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A frayed electrical cord is a shock and fire hazard; the aide removes the device from use and reports it for repair or replacement. Why the others are wrong: **A** continuing to use damaged equipment risks electrical injury or fire; **B** taping a frayed cord is an unsafe makeshift fix; **D** disabling the call light removes the resident's only way to summon help.

questions.stem: A resident has a blistered, reddened area on the heel after a hot pack was left on too long. How should the nurse aide document and handle this finding?

options.text: Write 'the resident was burned by careless staff' in the chart
Objectively describe and report what is observed (location, size, appearance) to the nurse, without guessing the cause
Do not document it to avoid getting anyone in trouble
Apply an ointment and bandage and say nothing

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Documentation and reporting should be objective and factual—what the aide actually observes (site, size, appearance)—and reported promptly to the nurse, without drawing conclusions about cause. Why the others are wrong: **A** assigning blame in the chart is subjective and inappropriate; **C** failing to document a skin injury is falsification by omission and unsafe; **D** applying medication is outside the aide's scope and hiding the finding endangers the resident.

questions.stem: A nurse aide must doff (remove) contaminated personal protective equipment after leaving an isolation room. Place the steps in the correct removal order.

options.text: Remove gloves
Remove goggles or face shield
Remove the gown
Remove the mask or respirator, then perform hand hygiene

questions.explanation: The correct doffing sequence is gloves, then goggles/face shield, then gown, then mask/respirator, finishing with hand hygiene. Gloves are removed first because they are the most contaminated. Eye protection and the gown come off next, touching only the clean inner surfaces. The mask or respirator is removed last—handled by its ties or straps—because the area in front of the face may carry airborne particles, and hand hygiene is performed immediately afterward.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is caring for a resident on oxygen by nasal cannula. Which two safety measures apply to oxygen use? (Select two.)

options.text: Keep open flames, smoking, and lit candles away from the resident's area
Adjust the oxygen flow rate up or down based on how the resident looks
Make sure 'Oxygen in Use' signs are posted and the tubing is not kinked
Apply petroleum jelly to the resident's nose for comfort

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Oxygen supports combustion, so flames and smoking must be kept away, signage posted, and the tubing kept unkinked so oxygen flows freely. Why the others are wrong: **B** changing the oxygen flow rate is a nurse's responsibility, not the aide's; **D** petroleum-based products near oxygen are flammable and should not be used—water-based lubricant is preferred.

questions.stem: A nurse aide finds a sharp disposable razor and a broken glass thermometer in a resident's room. How should these be discarded?

options.text: Place them in the regular trash can
Wrap them in tissue and put them in a pocket until later
Put sharp items in the labeled sharps (puncture-resistant) container per facility policy
Hand them directly to the resident to throw away

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Sharps such as razors and broken glass go into a labeled, puncture-resistant sharps container to prevent injuries and exposure. Why the others are wrong: **A** sharps in regular trash can cut and infect staff handling the bag; **B** carrying sharps in a pocket risks a puncture injury; **D** giving sharps to a resident is unsafe and inappropriate.

questions.stem: A resident is participating in a bladder-retraining program. Which action by the nurse aide best supports the program?

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter so toileting is not needed
Offer toileting on the scheduled times in the plan and praise successes
Limit the resident's fluids sharply throughout the day
Place the resident in disposable briefs and stop offering the toilet

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Bladder retraining relies on offering the toilet at the scheduled intervals in the care plan and giving positive encouragement when the resident succeeds. Why the others are wrong: **A** inserting a catheter is outside the aide's scope and works against retraining; **C** sharply restricting fluids can cause dehydration and concentrated urine; **D** relying on briefs and abandoning the toileting schedule undermines the goal of regaining control.

questions.stem: A resident recovering from a stroke uses a plate guard and built-up utensil handles at meals. What is the purpose of these adaptive devices?

options.text: To allow the resident to feed themselves more independently despite limited hand function
To make the meal look more decorative
To restrain the resident's hands during meals
To replace the need for the resident to eat

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Adaptive devices such as plate guards and built-up handles help residents with limited grip or coordination eat by themselves, promoting independence. Why the others are wrong: **B** the purpose is function, not decoration; **C** these devices aid eating, they do not restrain; **D** the resident still eats—the devices simply make self-feeding possible.

questions.stem: When assisting a resident who uses a cane on the stronger side, how should the resident be taught to go up stairs?

options.text: Lead with the weaker leg going up
Step up with the stronger leg first, then bring up the weaker leg and the cane
Carry the cane and hop up on one foot
Go up backward to be safe

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Going up stairs, the resident leads with the stronger leg, then brings up the weaker leg and the cane ('up with the good'). Why the others are wrong: **A** leading up with the weaker leg places the load on the impaired side and is unsafe; **C** hopping while carrying the cane removes support and risks a fall; **D** climbing stairs backward is unnecessary and dangerous.

questions.stem: A resident with dementia repeatedly asks to 'go home to see mother,' though the resident's mother died years ago. What is the most therapeutic response by the nurse aide?

options.text: Bluntly remind the resident that their mother is dead
Use a calm, reassuring tone and gently redirect, acknowledging the feeling behind the request
Argue until the resident accepts the truth
Ignore the resident completely

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** With a resident who has dementia, a calm tone, acknowledging the underlying emotion, and gentle redirection reduce distress, rather than forcing reality. Why the others are wrong: **A** bluntly stating the mother is dead can cause fresh grief and agitation repeatedly; **C** arguing increases confusion and anxiety; **D** ignoring the resident is neglectful and worsens distress.

questions.stem: A resident tells the nurse aide, 'I just want it all to be over. There's no point anymore.' What should the aide do?

options.text: Promise to keep it a secret and say nothing
Tell the resident not to talk that way and change the subject
Stay with the resident, take the statement seriously, and report it to the nurse right away
Assume the resident is only seeking attention and ignore it

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A statement suggesting hopelessness or possible suicidal thoughts is taken seriously; the aide stays with the resident, does not leave them alone, and reports it to the nurse immediately. Why the others are wrong: **A** promising secrecy can endanger the resident's life; **B** dismissing the comment shuts down communication and misses a warning sign; **D** assuming attention-seeking and ignoring it can have tragic consequences.

questions.stem: A new resident appears anxious and overwhelmed on the first day in the facility. Which action by the nurse aide best helps the resident adjust?

options.text: Leave the resident alone all day to settle in
Tell the resident that complaining will not help
Orient the resident to the room and routines, introduce yourself, and answer questions patiently
Rush through admission tasks without explaining anything

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Orienting the new resident to surroundings and routines, introducing yourself, and patiently answering questions ease anxiety and support adjustment. Why the others are wrong: **A** leaving an anxious new resident alone all day can deepen fear and isolation; **B** dismissing concerns is unkind and unhelpful; **D** rushing without explanation increases confusion and stress.

questions.stem: A resident's culture values direct family involvement, and several relatives want to help with the resident's care and meals. How should the nurse aide respond?

options.text: Tell the family they are not allowed to be involved in any care
Welcome appropriate family involvement, respect the cultural value, and coordinate with the nurse and care plan
Insist the resident follow the aide's own family customs instead
Ignore the family's wishes because they are not staff

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Culturally sensitive care welcomes appropriate family participation, respects the resident's values, and coordinates involvement through the nurse and care plan. Why the others are wrong: **A** flatly barring family disrespects the resident's culture; **C** imposing the aide's own customs ignores the resident's heritage; **D** dismissing family wishes is culturally insensitive and may conflict with the resident's preferences.

questions.stem: A resident is dying, and the family asks to perform a quiet religious ritual at the bedside. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse aide?

options.text: Tell the family rituals are not permitted in the facility
Provide privacy and quiet, support the family's wishes, and inform the nurse
Continue loud routine tasks in the room during the ritual
Ask the family to leave so care can continue on schedule

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Honoring end-of-life beliefs means giving the family privacy and a quiet setting, supporting their ritual, and notifying the nurse. Why the others are wrong: **A** religious and cultural practices are respected, not forbidden; **C** continuing loud tasks is disrespectful during a sacred moment; **D** sending the family away to keep a schedule disregards the resident's and family's needs at end of life.

questions.stem: A resident has expressive aphasia after a stroke and struggles to find words. Which communication technique is most helpful?

options.text: Speak for the resident and finish all their sentences quickly
Raise your voice and repeat the same long question rapidly
Avoid talking to the resident since communication is difficult
Allow extra time, ask yes/no questions, and offer a communication board or gestures

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** With expressive aphasia, giving extra time, using yes/no questions, and offering tools like a communication board or gestures support understanding. Why the others are wrong: **A** finishing sentences for the resident removes their voice and may be wrong; **B** shouting and rushing add pressure without aiding word-finding; **C** avoiding communication isolates the resident and is the opposite of good care.

questions.stem: A nurse aide answers the unit telephone. Which response best demonstrates professional communication and protects confidentiality?

options.text: Share a resident's diagnosis with any caller who asks
Answer with only 'Yeah?' and give out room numbers
Put the caller on hold indefinitely and walk away
Identify the unit and yourself, be courteous, and refer clinical questions to the nurse

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Professional phone etiquette means identifying the unit and yourself, being courteous, and directing clinical or confidential questions to the nurse. Why the others are wrong: **A** disclosing a diagnosis to any caller breaches confidentiality; **B** a curt greeting and giving out information is unprofessional and unsafe; **C** abandoning the caller on hold is discourteous and could delay urgent communication.

questions.stem: When giving an end-of-shift report to the oncoming nurse aide, which two practices support accurate, professional communication? (Select two.)

options.text: Report specific, factual observations such as intake, output, and any changes you noticed
Share unrelated personal gossip about the residents
Communicate any tasks still needing to be done and report in a private area
Guess at information you are unsure about so the report sounds complete

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** A good hand-off gives specific, factual information (intake, output, changes) and flags unfinished tasks, delivered where others cannot overhear confidential details. Why the others are wrong: **B** gossip is unprofessional and breaches dignity; **D** guessing introduces errors—uncertain items should be checked or reported as unknown, not fabricated.

questions.stem: A resident asks the nurse aide to mail a sealed letter to a family member. What is the resident's right regarding personal mail?

options.text: Staff may open and read all resident mail before sending it
The resident has the right to send and receive mail privately and unopened
Residents are not allowed to send personal mail
The aide should read the letter to make sure it is appropriate

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Residents have the right to send and receive their mail privately and unopened, as part of their rights to privacy and communication. Why the others are wrong: **A** opening and reading a resident's mail violates privacy rights; **C** residents are entitled to communicate by mail; **D** screening a resident's personal letter intrudes on a protected right.

questions.stem: A resident wants to take part in deciding their daily schedule and activities. How should the nurse aide support this right?

options.text: Tell the resident the staff decides everything
Choose activities for the resident without asking
Discourage the resident from making any decisions
Involve the resident in choices about their care and daily routine whenever possible

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Residents have the right to make choices and participate in decisions about their own care and routine; the aide offers options whenever possible. Why the others are wrong: **A** telling the resident staff decides everything strips away autonomy; **B** choosing for the resident without asking ignores their right to self-determination; **C** discouraging decisions undermines the resident's independence and dignity.

questions.stem: Which two situations are examples of neglect that violate a resident's rights and must be reported? (Select two.)

options.text: Leaving an incontinent resident in a wet, soiled brief for a long time despite requests for help
Failing to reposition an immobile resident, leading to a worsening pressure injury
Offering a resident a choice of clothing each morning
Reporting a change in a resident's condition to the nurse promptly

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Neglect is the failure to provide needed care; leaving a resident soiled and not repositioning an immobile resident (causing skin breakdown) are both neglect and must be reported. Why the others are wrong: **C** offering clothing choices respects rights and is good care, not neglect; **D** promptly reporting a change is exactly what proper care requires.

questions.stem: A nurse aide makes a documentation error while charting intake on the paper record. What is the correct way to correct it?

options.text: Use correction fluid to cover the mistake completely
Erase or scribble out the entry so it cannot be read
Draw a single line through the error, write the correction, and initial and date it per policy
Tear out the page and start over

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A charting error is corrected by drawing a single line through it (keeping it legible), writing the correct entry, and initialing and dating the change, so the record stays accurate and accountable. Why the others are wrong: **A** correction fluid hides information and looks like tampering; **B** erasing or scribbling out makes the record unreadable and raises legal questions; **D** removing a page destroys part of the legal record.

questions.stem: A grateful resident offers the nurse aide a $50 cash tip for good care. According to ethical conduct, how should the aide respond?

options.text: Accept the cash quietly so the resident is not offended
Politely decline the money, explaining that staff are not permitted to accept tips, and thank the resident
Take the money but promise extra attention in return
Ask the resident for a larger amount

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Accepting money or gifts from residents is an ethical boundary violation; the aide kindly declines, explains the policy, and thanks the resident. Why the others are wrong: **A** quietly taking the cash still violates professional ethics; **C** promising extra care for payment creates favoritism and is unethical; **D** asking for more money is exploitation of the resident.

questions.stem: A nurse delegates a task to the nurse aide that the aide is trained to do but cannot finish before the end of the shift. What is the most professional action?

options.text: Leave without telling anyone the task is unfinished
Report to the nurse and oncoming staff that the task is incomplete so care continues
Chart that the task was completed even though it was not
Refuse the task entirely and walk away

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Accountability and teamwork require communicating an unfinished delegated task to the nurse and oncoming staff so the resident's care is not interrupted. Why the others are wrong: **A** leaving silently can cause a gap in care; **C** charting a task as done when it was not is falsification; **D** refusing a task within the aide's competence without cause neglects the resident and the team.

questions.stem: Which behavior best reflects professionalism for a nurse aide in a long-term care facility?

options.text: Arriving late frequently and discussing residents on social media
Being punctual and dependable, maintaining a neat appearance, and keeping resident information confidential
Skipping assignments when busy and blaming coworkers
Using a personal cell phone for calls during resident care

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Professionalism includes being punctual and reliable, maintaining a clean, appropriate appearance, and protecting resident confidentiality. Why the others are wrong: **A** chronic lateness and posting about residents are unprofessional and breach confidentiality; **C** skipping work and blaming others harms teamwork and resident care; **D** taking personal calls during care distracts from the resident and is unprofessional.

questions.stem: A resident has just finished a tub bath. To protect the resident's skin while drying, what should the nurse aide do?

options.text: Pat the skin dry gently, taking care to dry between the toes and within skin folds
Rub the skin briskly with a rough towel to dry it faster
Leave the skin damp so lotion absorbs better
Use a hair dryer on a hot setting directly on the skin

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Skin is patted dry gently, and moisture is removed from between the toes and within skin folds where dampness can cause breakdown and fungal growth. Why the others are wrong: **B** brisk rubbing with a rough towel can tear fragile skin; **C** leaving skin damp promotes maceration and infection in folds; **D** a hot hair dryer can burn the skin and is not used for routine drying.

questions.stem: A resident wears eyeglasses and asks the nurse aide to clean them. What is the correct way to clean and store eyeglasses?

options.text: Clean the lenses with a dry paper towel and set the glasses face-down on the lenses
Wash them in very hot water to remove all smudges
Clean the lenses as directed (such as with water or lens cleaner and a soft cloth) and store them in a case or resting on the frames
Wipe them on the corner of the bed sheet

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Eyeglasses are cleaned with the recommended cleaner or water and a soft cloth, then stored safely in a case or resting on their frames so the lenses are not scratched. Why the others are wrong: **A** a dry paper towel scratches lenses and resting glasses on the lenses damages them; **B** very hot water can warp frames and loosen lenses; **D** a bed sheet is abrasive and unsanitary.

questions.stem: A resident is unconscious and the care plan calls for mouth care. To prevent aspiration during oral care, how should the nurse aide position the resident?

options.text: Flat on the back with the head straight
Sitting fully upright with the neck flexed forward
On the side with the head turned to the side
In a head-down position so fluids drain toward the throat

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** For an unconscious resident, mouth care is done with the resident on their side and the head turned to the side so fluids drain out of the mouth rather than into the airway. Why the others are wrong: **A** lying flat lets fluid pool at the back of the throat and be aspirated; **D** a head-down tilt directs fluids toward the throat; **B** an unconscious resident cannot be safely held fully upright and the position does not protect the airway like side-lying does.

questions.stem: A resident is on a low-sodium (low-salt) diet. Which action by the nurse aide best supports this diet at mealtime?

options.text: Serve the meal as ordered and do not add salt, reporting if the resident refuses to eat it
Add table salt to make the food taste better
Bring the resident salty snacks from the vending machine
Tell the resident the diet does not really matter

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The aide serves the diet exactly as ordered, withholds added salt, and reports poor intake or refusal so the team can respond. Why the others are wrong: **B** adding table salt defeats the purpose of the low-sodium order; **C** salty snacks violate the prescribed diet; **D** dismissing the diet ignores a medical order that may protect the resident's heart or kidneys.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is assisting a resident who must be weighed daily because of fluid concerns. The resident has had a large, watery stool and the brief is heavily soiled. What should the aide do before weighing?

options.text: Provide perineal care and a clean, dry brief, then weigh the resident under the usual conditions
Weigh the resident in the soiled brief to save time
Skip the weight for the day without telling anyone
Subtract an estimated amount for the soiled brief

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The resident is cleaned and placed in a dry brief, then weighed under the same conditions used each day so the daily weight is accurate and comparable. Why the others are wrong: **B** a soiled, wet brief adds weight and distorts the reading; **C** silently skipping a daily weight ordered for fluid monitoring omits important data; **D** guessing a deduction introduces error into a measurement used for medical decisions.

questions.stem: While giving care, a nurse aide notices a resident's fingernails are long and have dark debris underneath. The resident has no diabetes or circulatory problems and the care plan permits routine nail care. What is appropriate?

options.text: Clean under the nails and file them smooth as routine hygiene, reporting anything unusual
Leave the nails alone because nail care is never an aide's task
Bite the nails short for the resident
Use scissors to cut deep into the corners of each nail

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For a resident without diabetes or poor circulation, routine fingernail hygiene—cleaning beneath the nails and filing them smooth—is within the aide's role, with anything abnormal reported. Why the others are wrong: **B** routine fingernail care is allowed for residents who are not high-risk; **D** cutting deep into the corners can cause injury and ingrown nails; **C** biting a resident's nails is unsanitary and unprofessional.

questions.stem: A resident is incontinent of urine and the nurse aide is providing incontinence care. Which two actions best protect the resident's skin? (Select two.)

options.text: Cleanse the skin promptly after each episode and pat it thoroughly dry
Apply a moisture barrier product as directed by the care plan
Leave the wet brief on until it is completely saturated to reduce changes
Scrub the reddened skin vigorously to stimulate circulation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Prompt cleansing and thorough drying remove irritating moisture, and a care-plan-directed moisture barrier protects the skin from breakdown. Why the others are wrong: **C** leaving urine against the skin causes maceration and skin breakdown; **D** vigorous scrubbing damages already-fragile or reddened skin rather than protecting it.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is recording urinary output for a resident using a graduated container. The resident voided into a bedpan. How should the aide measure and record the output?

options.text: Pour the urine into a graduated measuring container at eye level, read the volume, and record it in milliliters
Estimate the amount by looking at the bedpan and round to the nearest cup
Record the output only if the urine looks abnormal
Add the urine to the next void before measuring so it is done once

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Urinary output is measured by pouring it into a graduate, reading the level at eye level on a flat surface, and recording the exact amount in milliliters. Why the others are wrong: **B** estimating from the bedpan is inaccurate; **C** all output is recorded, not only abnormal-looking urine; **D** combining separate voids before measuring loses the accuracy and timing the I&O record needs.

questions.stem: A resident reports being unable to fall asleep because of pain in the hip. The nurse aide has already repositioned the resident for comfort. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give the resident a pain pill from the medication cart
Tell the resident that everyone has aches at night
Report the resident's pain to the nurse so it can be evaluated and treated
Encourage the resident to walk laps until tired enough to sleep

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** After providing comfort measures within the aide's scope, unrelieved pain is reported to the nurse, who can assess it and arrange treatment. Why the others are wrong: **A** giving medication is outside the aide's scope; **B** dismissing the pain ignores a real symptom that affects rest; **D** walking on a painful hip at night is unsafe and does not address the pain.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is washing the hands at the sink with soap and water. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Wet the hands and wrists with warm running water, keeping the hands lower than the elbows
Apply soap and rub all surfaces, including between the fingers and under the nails, for at least 20 seconds
Rinse the hands and wrists thoroughly under running water, fingertips pointing down
Dry the hands with a clean paper towel and use a fresh towel to turn off the faucet

questions.explanation: The correct handwashing sequence is to wet the hands first with the hands held lower than the elbows so water runs from the cleaner forearms toward the dirtier hands. Soap is then applied and all surfaces are scrubbed for at least 20 seconds to loosen and remove microorganisms. Rinsing follows with the fingertips pointing down so contaminated water flows off the fingertips. Finally the hands are dried with a clean paper towel, and a fresh towel is used to turn off the faucet so the just-cleaned hands are not recontaminated.

questions.stem: A nurse aide is handling heavily soiled linens in a resident's room under standard precautions. Which two practices are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: Roll the linens with the soiled side turned inward
Hold the linens away from the uniform and place them in the proper hamper without shaking
Shake the linens out to remove debris before bagging them
Place the soiled linens on the floor until they can be collected
